International Workshop Highlights Artificial Intelligence Advances in Breast Cancer Risk Prediction

Researchers presenting at the 11th International Breast Density and Cancer Risk Assessment Workshop in Līhuʿe, Hawaii, reported that incorporating longitudinal screening records significantly improves five-year breast cancer risk prediction compared to evaluating single mammograms. Investigators led by Dr. Shu Jiang from Washington University School of Medicine, alongside collaborators from Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Weill Cornell Medicine, addressed the limitation that existing image-based risk models do not fully exploit historical imaging data. To develop a dynamic risk prediction model, the research team analyzed a prospective clinic-based cohort comprising 10,099 cancer-free women who enrolled during routine screening between November 3, 2008, and February 2012 at Washington University. Longitudinal follow-up through 2020 identified 478 pathology-confirmed breast cancer cases within this primary development cohort, which included 27 percent non-Hispanic Black women.

The dynamic model was independently evaluated across two external cohorts. In the Emory cohort of 18,360 women screened between 2013 and 2020, with 42 percent non-Hispanic Black participants and 332 pathology-confirmed breast cancers, incorporating three years of prior mammograms yielded a five-year area under the curve of 0.80 controlling for age and BI-RADS density, excluding cases diagnosed within six months of screening. This significantly outperformed the current screening visit alone, which achieved an area under the curve of 0.74. In the British Columbia Cancer cohort of 208,313 women aged 40 to 74 screened between 2013 and 2019, with 3,021 pathology-confirmed incident cases identified through June 2023, using up to four years of prior images generated an area under the curve of 0.78, exceeding the single-visit baseline of 0.71. Calibrated to SEER incidence rates, risk ratios comparing high-risk women exceeding four percent five-year risk against very low-risk women under 0.3 percent reached 21.1 in Emory and 24.4 in British Columbia.

Complementing longitudinal modeling, a multi-institutional analysis led by Dr. Graham A. Colditz evaluated whether an artificial intelligence-derived Mammogram Risk Score summarizing mammographic texture maintains generalizability across diverse racial and ethnic groups. Analyzing data from over 226,000 women across the Emory and British Columbia cohorts, the study examined score distributions among non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, East Asian, South Asian, and Indigenous women. The investigators observed minimal variation in median score distributions between the two cohorts overall, across distinct racial and ethnic groups within each cohort, and between cohorts within corresponding demographic categories. Proportional hazards regression demonstrated that each standard deviation increase in the risk score was significantly associated with elevated breast cancer risk, yielding age-adjusted hazard ratios ranging from 2.03 to 2.15. Stratified analyses confirmed consistent associations across populations, with hazard ratios of 2.12 for non-Hispanic Black women, 2.10 for East Asian women, 2.09 for South Asian women, and 2.19 for Indigenous women. Five-year discriminatory accuracy showed no statistically significant differences by race or ethnicity within each cohort.

Addressing screening policy, researchers from the University of Western Australia and BreastScreen Western Australia reported interval cancer detection patterns following breast density notification. The investigators evaluated 300,787 screening records among 214,712 clients in the state-wide screening program between 2016 and 2019, calculating interval cancer rates per 10,000 client-years stratified by diagnosis timing within 0 to 12 months versus 13 to 24 months post-screening. Clients notified of dense breasts experienced interval cancer detection rates two to six times higher than women not flagged with dense breasts. For the 2016 through 2018 period following a normal mammogram, estimated interval cancer rates were higher in the first year than in the second year among notified women, recording 27.8 versus 20.4 per 10,000 client-years overall, and 32.4 versus 18.6 among first-time attendees. During 2017 through 2019, rates were 16.5 per 10,000 client-years in months 0 to 12 compared with 15.2 in months 13 to 24, contrasting with national reports where interval cancer rates typically rise in the second year.

In personalized prevention, investigators presented the protocol of the RENAISSANCE trial, a phase II study evaluating adaptive tamoxifen dosing in premenopausal women at elevated breast cancer risk. Led by Dr. Seema A. Khan from Northwestern University across ten United States sites, the trial recruits 200 premenopausal candidates without previous invasive breast cancer, prior tamoxifen use, or contraindications. Participants initiate therapy at 5 milligrams daily, followed by repeat mammography at six months to evaluate absolute dense area reduction using the Karolinska STRATUS algorithm. Non-responders, defined as reduction of 10 percent or less and expected in 30 percent of participants, escalate to 10 milligrams daily, and to 20 milligrams daily if reduction remains under 10 percent at 12 months. With 82 percent power to detect an increase in responder fraction from 70 to 80 percent, the trial also analyzes serial blood samples, paired core biopsies, and endoxifen levels.

Investigating biological mechanisms underpinning image analysis, epidemiologists from Karolinska Institutet and the University of Cambridge applied causal mediation modeling to assess whether artificial intelligence scores capture established modifiable risk factors. Utilizing a case-cohort design from the Swedish KARMA screening cohort, the team followed 2,985 subcohort participants and 500 incident breast cancer cases across a median 10-year follow-up ending in June 2022. Absolute ten-year risk scores calculated from baseline mammograms mediated substantial proportions of risk attributable to clinical and lifestyle factors. Among postmenopausal participants, the image-derived score significantly mediated 58.1 percent of risk associated with body weight, 36.1 percent of risk linked to breast density, 31.8 percent of risk from benign breast disease, and 23.8 percent of risk conferred by family history. In premenopausal women, the model significantly mediated 26.8 percent of density-associated risk, 36.1 percent of benign breast disease risk, and 18.9 percent of family history risk, suggesting deep learning algorithms process structural alterations reflecting modifiable exposures and disease precursors.

Exploring deep neural networks, computational researchers from the University of Hawaiʻi Cancer Center and collaborating institutions examined unsupervised feature clustering to improve the explainability of cancer risk predictions. Working with the multiethnic Hawaiʻi and Pacific Islands Mammography Registry, the research team identified a sample of 3,776 matched controls and 1,307 invasive breast cancer cases diagnosed at least six months following four-view examinations. The investigators structured their analytical framework to correlate these computational clusters against clinical parameters, including body mass index, quantitative breast density categories, self-reported race and ethnicity, and five-year risk predictions. Planned statistical evaluations utilize Kruskal-Wallis testing, chi-squared contingency analyses, and Cox proportional hazards regression to determine whether specific latent image clusters correspond to distinct long-term cancer risk trajectories across ancestrally diverse screening populations.

Screening workflow integration was evaluated in a retrospective study conducted at Lund University and Skåne University Hospital in Malmö, Sweden. Researcher
